column3: Extends the nearby warning: revelation can be withdrawn and no effective advocate remains.
Frames life, death, and return as one divine sequence, supporting the two-domain consequence.
Pairs direct tasting of punishment with the absence of any helper.
Supplies a punishment setting explicitly marked by the absence of a helper.
Gives the immediate pressure to depart from what was revealed, the condition presupposed by 17:75.
Places life and death under the one who remains inheritor, grounding their joined scope.
Shows a failed opposing force left without protector or helper; a parallel aid-collapse scene.
Makes life, death, and renewed life a connected sequence rather than isolated states.
Provides the contrary prophetic pattern: enmity occurs alongside divine guidance and help.
Links divine rejection with finding no helper, though in a different moral setting.
States the prior divine stabilization whose absence would trigger the conditional punishment.
Contrasts the first death with protection from punishment, sharpening the death-side horizon.
Depicts intrinsic weakness, but does not materially specify 17:75's doubled consequence.
Continues the same pressure-and-consequence passage with a distinct displacement outcome.
Offers a secondary reading of doubled punishment through compounded responsibility across groups.
Joins enduring punishment to the permanent loss of protector and helper.
Shows punitive continuity as neither death nor life, qualifying the death-side experience.
Supplies a secondary, non-identical use of multiplication as compounding rather than two realms.
Links death to later full recompense, making the two-stage horizon explicit.
Keeps 17:75 inside the passage's unchanging divine practice for messengers.
Affirms life and death are governed beyond human escape, but adds little to punishment or help.
Uses weakness across life stages without addressing doubled tasting or unavailable help.
Contributes the life/death contrast, including a possible nonliteral receptive-closed reading.
Limits human control over the place of death, reinforcing the non-self-directed outcome.
Makes death a universal threshold followed by return, directly supporting a two-stage scope.
Adds a secondary life/death reading as responsiveness versus closure.
Confirms tasting as punitive experience, though its setting is otherwise remote.
Its life-bound punishment and appointment do not clarify the focus's double scope or no-helper clause.
Makes tasting punishment the earned outcome, completing the preceding doubled-punishment exchange.
Exposes the terminal failure of mutual aid, directly paralleling no helper.
Provides a contrary positive account in which effective help answers oppression.
Contrasts worldly life with a fuller later life, supporting a multi-domain horizon.
Distinguishes a nearer tasting from a greater one, adding a graded consequence reading.
Sets worldly tasting beside a more humiliating later punishment and lack of aid.
Separates apparent numbers from real helping strength, sharpening the no-helper clause.
Supplies the contrary case of divinely helped messengers.
Contrasts worldly life with the later horizon but does not specify the focus's consequence.
Uses revivified earth as a life/death sign; it is remote from punitive doubling.
Contrasts tasted mercy and later severe tasting, adding an experiential consequence pattern.
No path is found after misguidance, a loose parallel to loss of aid.
Clarifies enduring punishment by excluding both death and any reduction of its burden.
Shows tasting as the exposure of a prohibited act's consequence.
Connects worldly conduct to return and report, without the focus's double or aid elements.
Affirms that the declared consequence must be tasted, though with little further specification.
The guidance and protector language does not materially illuminate the focus's punishment pattern.
Affirms one authority over death and life, supporting their joined mention.
Social weakness in a local conflict does not clarify the focus.
Closely parallels stabilization followed by slipping and tasted evil for obstructing the path.
The challenge to messengerhood adds no relevant consequence or aid pattern.
Offers a contrasting appeal for divine help against corruption.
The repeated warning formula adds no determinate reading beyond earlier punishment cards.
Keeps living and dead within one earthly order but gives no consequence structure.
Contrasts the small worldly portion with the later one, only loosely related.
Shows divine punishment and help operating through human action, a secondary aid pattern.
The isolated warning formula is redundant and non-specific here.
Resurrection imagery supports life-after-death generally but is remote from the conditional warning.
Directly links death and subsequent life under one agent.
Depicts the day when even close relations cannot help one another.
Within the same surah, portrays exposure to punishment without an advocate.
Combines divine control of life and death with the absence of any other ally or helper.
Keeps the focus in its Quranic-recitation setting, though without a direct consequence link.
Makes the rejected punishment a commanded direct experience.
Places punishment in worldly life and a harsher later domain, with no protection.
Provides the contrary principle that real victory comes only from God.
Explicitly distributes severe punishment across worldly and later domains and denies helpers.
Records a claim of collective self-help, a weak contrary to its later collapse.
Within the surah, denies recourse against God after destructive punishment.
Questions whether any force besides God can provide effective help.
Associates entry into the fire with disgrace and absence of helpers.
Denies both ally and helper outside God, without the focus's life/death frame.
Relates the promised punishment to exposure of weaker supporting forces.
Again makes warning become personally tasted punishment; parallel but cumulative.
Supplies a distinct doubled-punishment reading through leaders' compounded responsibility.
Closes both aid to others and self-rescue for claimed intermediaries.
Combines painful punishment with finding neither ally nor helper.
Denies any other ally or helper, a general parallel.
The divine claim over guidance does not specify the focus's consequence.
Adds individual accountability and no helpers for wrongdoers, but only indirectly.
Links doing wrong to requital without any ally or helper.
Combines collapse of escape and aid with directly tasted great punishment.
Reinforces fidelity to revealed speech and lack of refuge, echoing the antecedent pressure.
Misguided desire and lack of helpers form only a distant secondary parallel.
The statement about divine explanation does not clarify the focus.
Shows an entire promised support network failing in every tested direction.
Sets worldly disgrace before a greater later punishment, an experiential two-stage parallel.
Defines help as dependent on God, a contrary framework for the focus's withdrawal of aid.
Divine accounting is too general to add to the specified punishment.
Frames rejecting the vulnerable as leaving one exposed before God without support.
Supplies the contrary pattern of divine rescue for messengers and believers.
Denies transferable rescue on the day of reckoning, sharpening individual no-help.
Joins life, death, and final destination under one divine act.
Makes death an unavoidable meeting followed by accounting, reinforcing the later horizon.
Denies burden-transfer and ends in return to God, a responsibility-side parallel.
Demonstrates restoration after death but does not illuminate punitive doubling or help.
Explicitly distinguishes the life and death of wrongdoers from the faithful, supporting paired domains.
Exposes the futility of acquired objects of help, a parallel to no helper.
General divine ownership and command add no focused interpretive distinction.
Treats life and death as transformable states and ends in emergence, supporting their connection.
Its plot-and-reversal theme does not add to the focus.
Provides the contrary consummation in which death no longer governs the rescued.
In the same surah's messenger context, supplies the contrary appeal for a divinely granted supporting authority.
Sets out death, life, death, renewed life, and return as a single sequence.
Adds a distinct twice-punished pattern before a further great punishment.
Pairs worldly punishment with dying in disbelief, a partial life-to-death consequence pattern.
Repeats the worldly-punishment and death-in-disbelief pattern in a second context.
Directly combines multiplied punishment with the absence of allies besides God.
Depicts the terminal collapse of mutual rescue between the misleader and those who followed.
Adds compounded liability: bearing one's own burdens together with burdens caused in others.
Explicitly increases punishment for disbelief joined to blocking the divine path.
Denies protector and intercessor for a soul handed over to what it earned.
Places humiliating punishment at the taking of souls, sharpening the death-side horizon.
Shows punishment directly accompanying the taking of disbelievers' souls.
Joins worldly disgrace to a later tasted fire-punishment for turning from the path.
Explicitly multiplies punishment and makes its humiliating condition enduring.
Supplies doubled punishment as a heightened-responsibility pattern within the prophetic household.
Uses a request for doubled fire-punishment to distinguish responsibility between parties.
Names two deaths and two lives, a direct secondary configuration for the paired terms.
Stages punishment before and at the Hour, expanding the temporal range of punitive experience.
Denies a useful excuse and gives wrongdoers a cursed, worst destination on the decisive day.
Places Hell ahead of its subjects and denies any protector from what they acquired.
Depicts punishment at death as angels take souls, providing a direct death-side parallel.
Marks the punitive setting by the absence of any devoted friend.
Makes the decisive day one in which no soul can act for another, reinforcing no-help.
